title: Frameworks 101
subtitle: How cybersecurity and IT frameworks work
source: Based on NIST CSWP 29, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, NIST AI 100-1 and public framework documentation
description: Start here. What frameworks are, how they are structured, and how NIST CSF 2.0, SP 800-53 and the AI RMF fit together.

chapters.title: What a framework is
chapters.summary: Frameworks, standards, regulations and control catalogs, and why the difference matters.

blocks.text: A **framework** is a structured, reusable way of organising what an organisation should achieve (and sometimes how) in a given domain, such as cybersecurity, IT service delivery or AI risk. It gives everyone a shared vocabulary, a shared structure and a shared yardstick.

Think of it as the table of contents for a discipline. It tells you which topics must be covered and how they relate, so that a CISO, an auditor, a regulator and an engineer can point at the same box and mean the same thing.

blocks.title: Why executives care
blocks.text: A framework turns a vague question ("Are we secure?") into a measurable one ("How far are we from our target on each of these 106 outcomes, and what does closing the gap cost?"). That is what makes security fundable and reportable to a board.
What a framework is not

items: It is not a product. No tool makes you "CSF compliant" out of the box.
It is not a one-off project. Frameworks assume a cycle: assess, improve, re-assess.
It is not automatically a legal obligation. Most frameworks are voluntary until a regulator, contract or customer makes them mandatory.

blocks.text: These words get used interchangeably in meetings. They are not the same, and mixing them up leads to bad scoping decisions.

rows: High-level structure of outcomes or practices. Flexible, adaptable.
NIST CSF 2.0, NIST AI RMF, COBIT 2019, ITIL
Formal document with specific requirements, often certifiable by an accredited body.
Voluntary, unless required by contract or law
GDPR, EU AI Act, Mauritius Data Protection Act 2017, Saudi PDPL
Detailed list of safeguards (controls) you can select from.
Mandatory for US federal systems; voluntary elsewhere
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CIS Controls v8.1, ISO/IEC 27002
NIST SP 800-61 (incident handling), ITIL practice guides

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Frameworks tell you **what** good looks like. Control catalogs tell you **how** to get there. Standards let a third party **certify** that you got there. Regulations tell you what happens if you don't.

items: **Common language.** Business, IT, security, audit and regulators discuss the same structure.
**Completeness.** A framework is a checklist of domains that mature organisations have learned the hard way not to forget (for example, supply chain risk or recovery communications).
**Prioritisation.** Comparing current state against a target shows where money and effort buy the most risk reduction.
**Assurance.** Customers, regulators and insurers accept evidence mapped to a known framework faster than a home-grown story.
**Benchmarking.** You can compare business units, subsidiaries or peers on the same scale.
**Career and hiring.** Roles, skills and certifications align to recognised frameworks, which simplifies building teams.

blocks.title: Example: a regional bank
blocks.text: A bank operating in several African markets faces different central-bank cyber directives in each country. Instead of running five separate programmes, it anchors on NIST CSF 2.0 as its internal operating model and maps each regulator's requirements to CSF subcategories. One programme, many reports.
The single most useful distinction when you pick up any new framework is whether it describes **outcomes** or prescribes **activities and controls**.

rows: "Users, services and hardware are authenticated" (CSF PR.AA-03)
"Implement multi-factor authentication for access to privileged accounts" (SP 800-53 IA-2(1))
Adapts to any size, sector, technology
Can become box-ticking; may not fit your context
NIST CSF 2.0, NIST AI RMF, COBIT objectives
NIST SP 800-53, CIS Controls, PCI DSS

blocks.text: Most real programmes combine both: an outcome framework to decide **what** matters and set targets, and a control catalog to decide **how** to meet each outcome.
Only some frameworks lead to an organisational certificate. This matters when a client asks "Are you certified?"

rows: Surveillance audits yearly, recertification every 3 years
Self-assessment or third-party assessment against CSF
No certificate; US federal systems receive an Authorization to Operate (ATO)
ISO/IEC 20000-1 certifies the service management system
Not a certification; an attestation report by a CPA firm
Type I (design) or Type II (operating effectiveness)

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: "We are NIST certified" is a red flag in a proposal. NIST does not certify organisations. Say "aligned to" or "assessed against" NIST CSF 2.0.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes a framework?
options: A structured, reusable way to organise outcomes or practices in a domain
A software tool that enforces controls
quiz.explain: Frameworks give structure and shared vocabulary. Laws carry penalties; tools and settings implement controls.

quiz.q: NIST SP 800-53 is best classified as a...
quiz.explain: SP 800-53 is a catalog of security and privacy controls. It is mandatory for US federal systems, voluntary for everyone else.

quiz.q: Which of these can an organisation be formally certified against?
quiz.explain: ISO/IEC 27001 has accredited third-party certification. NIST frameworks and ITIL do not certify organisations.

quiz.q: "Users, services and hardware are authenticated" is an example of...
quiz.explain: It describes a result, not the mechanism. This is CSF 2.0 subcategory PR.AA-03.

quiz.q: A client says their firm is 'NIST certified'. What is the most accurate response?
options: That is the highest level of assurance
NIST does not certify organisations; ask what assessment was done and by whom
quiz.explain: NIST publishes frameworks; it does not run a certification scheme for organisations.

chapters.title: How frameworks work
chapters.summary: The anatomy shared by most frameworks: hierarchy, profiles, maturity, mappings and the improvement cycle.

blocks.text: Almost every framework is a tree. Learn to spot the levels and you can read any new framework in an afternoon.

blocks.title: Reading trick
blocks.text: The identifier tells you where you are. PR.AA-05 = PROTECT function, Identity Management, Authentication and Access Control category, outcome 05. AC-2(1) = Access Control family, control 2 (Account Management), enhancement 1.
No organisation needs every outcome at the same strength. Frameworks handle this through **tailoring**, usually expressed as **profiles**.

items: **Current profile:** where you are today for each outcome.
**Target profile:** where you need to be, driven by risk appetite, regulation and business priorities.
**Gap:** the difference, which becomes your roadmap.
**Community profile / baseline / overlay:** a pre-built target for a sector or use case, e.g. a CSF community profile for manufacturing, or the SP 800-53B moderate baseline.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: An oil & gas operator sets a high target for asset inventory and OT network monitoring (ID.AM, DE.CM) because of safety risk, and a moderate target for secure software development (PR.PS-06) because it buys most software rather than building it.
Many frameworks include a way to express **how well** you do something, not just **whether** you do it.

rows: Tiers 1 to 4: Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable, Adaptive
Rigor of risk governance and management practices
None formally; profiles express current vs target

blocks.title: CSF Tiers are not maturity levels
blocks.text: NIST is explicit that Tiers describe the rigor of risk practices and are not meant to be scored like a maturity model. Many consultancies still build 0-5 maturity scales on top of CSF. That is fine, just be clear it is your scale, not NIST's.

Because organisations follow several frameworks at once, publishers provide **crosswalks** (mappings) that show where requirements overlap. NIST calls these **Informative References** and publishes them through the OLIR program (Online Informative References).

rows: PR.AA-05 Access permissions follow least privilege

blocks.title: A mapping is not an equivalence
blocks.text: Two items mapped to each other overlap; they rarely say the same thing. Passing an ISO 27001 audit on control 8.13 does not prove you meet every aspect of CSF PR.DS-11 (e.g. testing restores). Use crosswalks to reduce duplicate effort, not to skip assessment.
Frameworks assume a loop, usually a variant of Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA):

items: **Scope:** decide which business units, systems and services are in.
**Understand context:** mission, obligations, risk appetite, threats.
**Assess current state** against the framework.
**Set the target state** for each outcome.
**Analyse gaps** and estimate cost and risk reduction of closing each one.
**Build and execute a roadmap.**
**Measure and report** progress with metrics.
**Repeat** when threats, business or technology change.

blocks.title: Board framing
blocks.text: Report the gap, the plan and the trend. Boards don't need 106 subcategories; they need the five or six risks that matter, what it costs to fix them and whether the trend is improving.

quiz.q: In the identifier PR.AA-05, what does 'PR' refer to?
quiz.explain: CSF identifiers start with the function code: GV, ID, PR, DE, RS, RC.

quiz.q: What is a target profile?
options: The desired state of outcomes based on risk, obligations and priorities
The result of a penetration test
quiz.explain: Current profile = today. Target profile = where you need to be. The gap drives the roadmap.

quiz.q: NIST CSF Tiers are best described as...
options: A description of the rigor of cybersecurity risk governance and management
quiz.explain: NIST says Tiers characterise rigor and are not a maturity model to be scored.

quiz.q: Two controls from different frameworks appear together in a crosswalk. This means...
options: Meeting one automatically meets the other
They overlap in intent, but each must still be assessed on its own terms
quiz.explain: Mappings show relationships, not equivalence.

quiz.q: Which step comes immediately after assessing the current state?
quiz.explain: You compare current to target to find gaps.

chapters.title: The NIST trio: CSF, SP 800-53 and AI RMF
chapters.summary: How the three NIST publications fit together: outcomes, controls and AI-specific risk.

blocks.text: The **National Institute of Standards and Technology** is a US federal agency under the Department of Commerce. Its cybersecurity publications are free, public domain and widely used far outside the US, including across the Middle East and Africa, because they are vendor-neutral and well maintained.

rows: AI 100-1: AI RMF 1.0; AI 600-1: Generative AI Profile
What cybersecurity outcomes should we achieve?
Which specific safeguards do we implement?
How do we govern and manage risk from AI systems?
AI developers, deployers, risk and governance teams
Yes for US federal systems; voluntary otherwise

blocks.text: Think of it as a building. **CSF** is the architect's brief: rooms the building must have and what they must do. **SP 800-53** is the building code and bill of materials: exact specifications you pick from. **AI RMF** is a specialist brief for a new kind of room (the AI system) whose risks behave differently: they are socio-technical, probabilistic and can change after deployment.
A worked example shows the chain from outcome to control to AI-specific risk.

items: **CSF outcome (what):** PR.AA-05: Access permissions, entitlements and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties.
**800-53 controls (how):** AC-2 Account Management, AC-5 Separation of Duties, AC-6 Least Privilege, including enhancement AC-6(5) Privileged Accounts.

**AI RMF lens (AI-specific):** if an AI agent is given access to the core banking system, GOVERN 1.4 and MAP 3.5 ask who approved its permissions, what human oversight exists, and MANAGE 2.4 asks how you would disengage it if it behaves outside its intended use.

blocks.title: Where AI meets cyber
blocks.text: AI RMF covers the full range of AI harms (bias, safety, privacy, explainability), not just security. For the security of AI systems specifically, you use CSF and 800-53 controls alongside it. NIST has been developing AI-specific control overlays for SP 800-53 and a Cyber AI profile of CSF to bridge the two; check NIST's site for their current status.
You will not study all of SP 800-53 here, but you need to know how it is built because CSF and AI RMF implementations lean on it.
The 20 control families
Anatomy of one control

items: **Control statement:** the requirement, often with organisation-defined parameters in brackets, e.g. "Review accounts for compliance with account management requirements [Assignment: organization-defined frequency]".
**Discussion:** rationale and implementation notes.
**Related controls:** links to other controls.
**Control enhancements:** stronger versions, e.g. AC-2(1) Automated System Account Management.
**References:** source standards.

blocks.text: Baselines and assessment

**SP 800-53B** defines starting sets of controls (baselines) for systems categorised as Low, Moderate or High impact, plus a privacy baseline. **SP 800-53A** explains how to assess each control (examine, interview, test).

Don't confuse **RMF** (SP 800-37, for managing security risk of information systems) with **AI RMF**. The RMF is the process that puts 800-53 controls to work on a specific system. It has seven steps:

rows: Establish context, roles, risk strategy at organisation and system level
Rate the system's impact (Low / Moderate / High) using FIPS 199 and SP 800-60
Pick a baseline from 800-53B and tailor it
Test whether controls are implemented correctly and effective (800-53A)
A senior official accepts residual risk and issues an Authorization to Operate (ATO)
Continuously track controls, changes and threats

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: CSF = organisation-wide outcomes. RMF = system-level lifecycle that selects and authorises 800-53 controls. AI RMF = AI-specific risk management across the AI lifecycle.

quiz.q: Which NIST publication is a catalog of security and privacy controls?
quiz.explain: SP 800-53 is the control catalog. CSWP 29 is CSF 2.0; AI 100-1 is AI RMF; SP 800-37 is the RMF process.

quiz.q: How many functions does the NIST AI RMF Core have?
quiz.explain: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE.

quiz.q: In SP 800-53, what is AC-6?
quiz.explain: AC-2 Account Management, AC-3 Access Enforcement, AC-5 Separation of Duties, AC-6 Least Privilege.

quiz.q: What does the 'Authorize' step of SP 800-37 produce?
options: An Authorization to Operate by a senior official accepting residual risk
quiz.explain: The authorising official formally accepts residual risk.

quiz.q: Which statement about AI RMF and CSF is most accurate?
options: AI RMF replaces CSF for AI systems
AI RMF covers broad AI harms; CSF and 800-53 still apply to securing the AI system
CSF 2.0 already covers bias and fairness
quiz.explain: They complement each other: AI RMF for trustworthiness and AI harms, CSF and 800-53 for cybersecurity outcomes and controls.

quiz.q: SP 800-53B provides...
options: Control baselines for Low, Moderate and High impact systems
quiz.explain: 800-53A = assessment procedures; 800-53B = baselines.

chapters.title: The wider landscape
chapters.summary: Where ISO 27001, COBIT, ITIL, CIS, SOC 2 and ISO 42001 fit, and how to choose.

Clauses 4-10 + Annex A: 93 controls in 4 themes (Organizational 37, People 8, Physical 14, Technological 34)
You need certification to win or keep clients
You need detailed control specifications or serve US government
You want a pragmatic, prioritised starting list, especially for SMEs
Enterprise governance of information and technology
40 objectives in 5 domains: EDM, APO, BAI, DSS, MEA
You need board-level IT governance and audit alignment

blocks.text: A useful mental model is three layers:

items: **Governance layer** (why and who decides): COBIT, CSF GOVERN, AI RMF GOVERN, ISO management-system clauses 4-10.
**Management layer** (what and how it's run): CSF functions, ITIL practices, ISO 27001 ISMS processes, AI RMF MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE.
**Control layer** (how, specifically): SP 800-53, ISO/IEC 27002, CIS Controls, PCI DSS requirements.

blocks.title: Example stack for a bank in MENA
blocks.text: COBIT for board-level IT governance, ISO/IEC 27001 for certification demanded by international correspondents, NIST CSF 2.0 as the internal security operating model and reporting language, CIS Controls to prioritise technical hardening, ITIL for service operations, and AI RMF plus ISO/IEC 42001 as AI use grows. Local regulation (e.g. SAMA Cyber Security Framework in Saudi Arabia) is mapped on top.

items: **Start from obligations.** Regulation and contracts are non-negotiable; map them first.
**Pick one anchor.** Choose a single framework as your internal operating model (CSF is a common choice) and map everything else to it.
**Add depth where needed.** Use a control catalog for implementation detail.
**Certify only when it pays.** Certification costs time and money; do it when clients or regulators value it.
**Avoid framework soup.** Running four frameworks as four separate programmes multiplies audits and confuses owners.

blocks.title: Pitfalls
blocks.text: Checkbox compliance (evidence without risk reduction), treating a framework as a project with an end date, copying a target profile from another organisation, and letting the tool vendor define your framework interpretation.
This library continues with the full NIST CSF 2.0, the full NIST AI RMF and ITIL (Version 5) Foundation. As you read, keep asking three questions of every outcome or practice:

items: What risk does this reduce?
What evidence would prove it is working?
Who owns it?

blocks.title: Build your own books
blocks.text: ISO/IEC 27001, COBIT 2019 and ISO/IEC 42001 are natural next books. Use the template in Settings to add them in the same format.

quiz.q: How many Annex A controls does ISO/IEC 27001:2022 contain?
quiz.explain: 93 controls in 4 themes. The 2013 edition had 114.

quiz.q: Which framework is primarily about enterprise governance of information and technology?
quiz.explain: COBIT, from ISACA, targets governance and management of enterprise IT.

quiz.q: Which is a certifiable AI management system standard?
quiz.explain: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 supports third-party certification.

quiz.q: What is the recommended way to handle several frameworks?
options: Run each as a separate programme
Pick one anchor framework and map the others to it
quiz.explain: An anchor plus mappings reduces duplication and keeps one language.

quiz.q: In the three-layer model, CIS Controls sit in which layer?
quiz.explain: CIS Controls are specific technical safeguards.

glossary.definition: A structured, reusable way of organising outcomes or practices in a domain.
A formal document with specific requirements, often certifiable (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001).
A safeguard or countermeasure that modifies risk.
A structured list of controls to select from (e.g. SP 800-53, CIS Controls).
In SP 800-53, a strengthened version of a base control, written as AC-2(1).
A predefined starting set of controls for a given impact level.
A tailored set of controls for a specific technology, sector or use case, applied on top of a baseline.
A mapping between requirements of two frameworks.

Authorization to Operate: a senior official's formal acceptance of a system's residual risk (SP 800-37).
Plan-Do-Check-Act, the improvement cycle behind most management frameworks.
